rules.title: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance Annual General Adjustment cap and formula
rules.requirement: For eligible fully covered units, Berkeley's Annual General Adjustment for 2026 allows a 1.0% increase to 2025 permanent rent ceilings no earlier than January 1, 2026. Measure BB also caps the Annual General Adjustment at 5%, while Berkeley Municipal Code section 13.76.110A ties the AGA to a CPI-based formula.
rules.key_value: 2026 AGA: 1.0%; maximum AGA: 5%; formula described as 65% of CPI
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to eligible landlords increasing rent ceilings for fully covered units.; Applies only to eligible landlords and qualifying tenancies under the AGA order.
rules.exemptions: The 2026 AGA may not adjust rents for tenants whose tenancy began on or after January 1, 2025 and whose rents were set pursuant to Costa-Hawkins.
rules.interaction: The 2026 AGA may not adjust tenants’ rents when their tenancy began on or after January 1, 2025, and who had their rents set pursuant to the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act.
rules.quoted_span:
At its regular meeting on October 16, 2025, the Berkeley Rent Stabilization Board 
adopted the Annual General Adjustment (AGA) Order for Year 2026 which will allow 
eligible landlords to increase the 2025 permanent rent ceilings by 1.0% no earlier than 
January 1, 2026. The 2026 AGA of 1.0% represents 65% of the increase in the Consumer 
Price Index (CPI) for All Urban Consumers in the Bay Area during the period from July 1, 
2024 - June 30, 2025, which was 1.5% as posted by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The 
65% of CPI formula was approved by Berkeley voters in the November 2004 general 
municipal election. See Berkeley Municipal Code section 13.76.110A. for rules related to 
establishing the AGA.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2024-12-20 (Notice-of-tenant-rights change date discussed on Measure BB page; not clearly stated as the effective date of the AGA cap itself, D006)

rules.title: Measure BB changes to Berkeley Rent Ordinance coverage affecting rent control applicability
rules.requirement: Measure BB changed which units are fully covered, partially covered, or exempt from Berkeley rent control, including some government-subsidized units and shared kitchen/bath units. Fully covered units have a rent ceiling and are subject to Berkeley's local rent increase limits; partially covered units are not subject to rent control.
rules.key_value: Coverage determines whether local rent ceiling/AGA applies; fully covered vs. partially covered vs. exempt
rules.coverage_conditions: Certain government-owned or -subsidized units are now fully or partially covered depending on unit type and other law.; Most units in multifamily properties built before 1980 are fully covered.; New construction units with a certificate of occupancy issued after June 1980 are partially covered.; Single-family homes with current tenancies that began before 1996 are fully covered.; Single-family homes with a tenancy that began on or after January 1, 1996 are partially covered.; Most condominiums are partially covered.
rules.exemptions: A unit where the owner shares a kitchen or bath with the tenant is exempt if the owner lived on the property when the tenancy started.; Golden duplexes are exempt.; Certain owner-occupied ADU properties are exempt for tenancies started after November 7, 2018.; University rental units such as dormitories are exempt.; Nonprofit cooperatives are exempt.
rules.interaction: Whether a unit is fully or partially covered depends on unit type and if Federal law, State law, or administrative regulation exempts the unit from the rent control provisions of Berkeley’s Rent Ordinance.
rules.quoted_span:
Units that are fully covered will have a rent ceiling, meaning rent increases will be limited by the
Annual General Adjustment
set by the Rent Board each year.
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents

rules.title: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance as amended by Measure BB
rules.requirement: Berkeley's Rent Ordinance provides just-cause eviction protections for fully and partially covered units, limits certain eviction grounds, imposes content and filing requirements for termination notices, and requires relocation assistance for owner move-in evictions with annual inflation adjustments.
rules.key_value: Just cause required for fully and partially covered units; nonpayment eviction barred for rental debt less than one month of equivalent-size HUD Fair Market Rent; eviction notice/lawsuit copies due to Rent Board within 3 business days; owner move-in relocation assistance adjusted annually, with 2026 amounts of $19,413 standard plus $6,471 additional for qualifying households.
rules.coverage_conditions: Fully covered units are covered by just-cause eviction protections.; Partially covered units are covered by just-cause eviction protections.; Single-family homes with tenancies beginning on or after January 1, 1996 are partially covered and subject to just-cause eviction protections.; Most condominiums are partially covered and subject to just-cause eviction protections.; Specified government-subsidized units are fully or partially covered depending on unit type or subsidy and therefore subject to just-cause eviction protections.
rules.exemptions: A unit where the owner shares a kitchen or bath with the tenant is exempt only if the owner lived on the property at the start of the tenancy.; A unit where the owner shares a kitchen or bath with the tenant is exempt only if the owner lived on the property at the start of the tenancy.; A golden duplex is exempt.; Tenancies started after November 7, 2018, on properties where one unit is an ADU and either unit is owner-occupied are exempt.; Tenancies started after November 7, 2018, on properties where one unit is an ADU and either unit is owner-occupied are exempt.; Tenancies started after November 7, 2018, on properties where one unit is an ADU and either unit is owner-occupied are exempt.; University rental units such as dormitories are exempt.; Nonprofit cooperatives are exempt.
rules.quoted_span: In Berkeley, tenants in units that are fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance cannot be evicted unless there is "just cause” (previously called “good cause”). Measure BB has changed some just causes, eliminated one just cause, added new requirements for eviction notices, and shortened the timeline for landlords to file copies of certain eviction-related documents with the Rent Board.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2026-01-01 (2026 relocation assistance adjustment effective date, D004); 2026-01-01 (2026 AGA effective no earlier than, D008); 2024-02-06 (utility-charge rule effective for tenancies starting on or after this date; not a just-cause rule, D006)

rules.title: Tenant screening fee disclosure requirement
rules.requirement: When an owner or agent charges an applicant a fee to purchase a consumer credit report and to validate, review, or otherwise process an application for Berkeley residential property, the owner must provide a clear and conspicuous tenant screening fee rights statement and the maximum fee cap permitted under state law, either in the rental application or in a separate disclosure before receiving the fee. An owner or agent may not charge an existing tenant a non-refundable fee to renew a tenancy, including fees tied to a roommate leaving or a request to add or replace a roommate in a pre-existing household. Chapter 13.78 applies to all residential rental agreements regardless of contrary lease language, and any lease provision that violates the chapter is unenforceable. This applicability rule governs Berkeley's local tenant screening and application fee provisions in Chapter 13.78.
rules.key_value: Disclosure required before receiving screening fee; must include rights statement and state-law maximum fee cap
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies when an owner or agent gets a request to rent residential property in Berkeley from an applicant and charges an application/screening fee.
rules.quoted_span: When an owner or the owner’s agent gets a request to rent residential property in Berkeley from an applicant and the owner charges a fee to purchase a consumer credit report and to validate, review, or otherwise process an application, the owner must provide, either in the rental application or in a separate disclosure before receiving the fee, a clear and conspicuous tenant screening fee rights statement and a statement of the maximum fee cap permitted under
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents

rules.title: Ronald V. Dellums Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance
rules.requirement: Berkeley prohibits rental housing providers from asking about or using criminal history or criminal background checks in rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection, or decision-making, and bars adverse actions based on criminal history subject to stated exceptions.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental housing providers in Berkeley.
rules.exemptions: Lifetime sex offenders.; Public housing/Section 8 properties have limited exemptions.; Owner-occupied properties between 1 and 3 units in which an owner of record resides in one unit as their primary residence.; Owner-occupied properties between 1 and 3 units in which an owner of record resides in one unit as their primary residence.; Owner-occupied properties between 1 and 3 units in which an owner of record resides in one unit as their primary residence.; Units under a rental agreement allowing owners to move back to their home in accordance with BMC 13.76.130 A.9.; Units occupied by existing tenant(s) seeking to sublet or add/replace roommates.
rules.quoted_span: The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2020-04-14 (passed by City Council, D003)
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents
rules.penalty: Administrative fines of at least $1,000 and up to $10,000 per violation, civil damages including actual damages or three times the amount of one month's rent, punitive damages, attorneys' fees and costs, and injunctive relief.

rules.title: Prohibition on sale or use of coordinated pricing algorithms for residential dwelling units
rules.requirement: Berkeley Municipal Code chapter 13.63 prohibits selling, licensing, or otherwise providing coordinated pricing algorithms to Berkeley landlords for setting or recommending rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in Berkeley, and prohibits landlords from using such algorithms for those purposes. The chapter defines covered algorithms and competitor data, excludes certain aggregated-data, affordable-housing, appraisal/financing, and software-development uses, and authorizes city and tenant civil actions with penalties up to $1,000 per violation.
rules.key_value: Civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; each separate month and each separate residential dwelling unit is a separate violation.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley.
rules.exemptions: Excluded are aggregated and anonymous rental-data products that do not recommend future lease terms.; Excluded are products used to establish rent or income limits under affordable housing guidelines of government entities.; Excluded are products or information used for project-financing market research, appraisals, or research, testing, or training for software development, so long as competitor data is not used as an input when a recommendation is calculated for publication or provision to a Berkeley landlord.
rules.interaction:
F. This Chapter is not intended to prevent the development or sale of software to help 
landlords manage their units generally or through the use of public data. Nor does this 
Chapter regulate the amount of rent that a landlord may charge. This Chapter solely 
regulates the use and sale of the coordinated pricing algorithms, to prevent the harms 
described above.
rules.quoted_span:
A. It shall be unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide to City of Berkeley 
landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy 
levels that may be achieved for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley. 
B. It shall be unlawful for a landlord to use a coordinated pricing algorithm described 
in subsection A when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in 
the City of Berkeley. Each separate month that a violation exists or continues, and each 
separate residential dwelling unit for which the landlord used the coordinated pricing 
algorithm, shall constitute a separate and distinct violation.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2025-11-18 (passed to print and ordered published, D001); 2026-01 (secondary source says effective January 2026, S002)
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents
rules.penalty: The City Attorney may seek damages, injunctive relief, restitution/return of illegal profits, and/or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation; aggrieved tenants may seek injunctive relief, money damages, and/or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation; prevailing city or tenant plaintiffs receive reasonable attorney’s fees and costs.

rules.title: Housing Stability Notification Act notice requirement when ending a tenancy
rules.requirement: Boston requires landlords planning to end a tenancy agreement to provide tenants with a Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources at the same time as a notice to quit or notice of non-renewal. The ordinance also requires landlords and foreclosing owners to notify the City and applies to all landlords/foreclosing owners ending a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy, subject to stated facility exemptions.
rules.key_value: Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources must be delivered at the same time as the Notice to Quit or Notice of non-renewal of lease; 2nd and subsequent offenses: $300 per day
rules.coverage_conditions: Landlords or foreclosing owners intending to end a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy of a unit in Boston
rules.exemptions: Residences in any hospital, skilled nursing facility or health facility; Residences in a non-profit facility whose primary purpose is providing short-term treatment, assistance or therapy for alcohol, drug, or other substance abuse
rules.interaction: If a landlord violates the HSNA, it DOES NOT halt the eviction process.
rules.quoted_span:
The HSNA requires that landlords give this Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources
to tenants when the landlord starts the eviction process, or when the landlord
decides to not offer the tenant a renewal of their lease agreement. The Notice of
Tenants’ Rights and Resources must be delivered at the same time as the Notice to
Quit.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2020-10 (passed by the City of Boston, D014)
rules.penalty: 1st Offense: Warning; 2nd and Subsequent Offenses: $300 per day

rules.title: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy
rules.requirement: Housing providers receiving specified City-linked funding, land, or inclusionary units may not use a blanket criminal-record denial policy and must assess applicants case by case. They may not consider arrests not resulting in conviction, convictions subject to judicial relief, juvenile records, or convictions more than 5 years old, and they may not use applicant credit score to approve or deny housing applications. Covered agents may not use an applicant credit score to approve or deny housing applications. They may consider credit history only in lieu of rental history to determine ability to pay rent when rental history is unavailable, and lack of credit history alone is not sufficient justification to reject an applicant.
rules.key_value: No blanket criminal-history denial; no convictions older than 5 years; no use of applicant credit score to approve or deny
rules.coverage_conditions: Housing providers receiving Department of Neighborhood Development funding and/or land; Housing providers with income restricted units created under the Boston Planning and Development Agency Inclusionary Development Policy
rules.exemptions: Direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought or unreasonable risk of substantial harm to the safety of others; Current criminal behavior
rules.interaction: Where federal or state law imposes a criminal history requirement that conflicts with a requirement of this guidance, the federal or state law preempts this policy.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy
rules.quoted_span:
Housing providers receiving Department of Neighborhood Development (DND) funding and/or 
land, or that have income restricted units created under the Boston Planning and Development 
Agency (BPDA) Inclusionary Development Policy will not impose a blanket policy that denies 
housing to anyone with arrests and or convictions. Housing providers will consider applicants on 
a case-by-case basis.
rules.raw_citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents

rules.title: Statewide rent cap for most residential real property
rules.requirement: California caps rent increases for covered residential units at no more than 5% plus the applicable cost-of-living change, or 10%, whichever is lower, over any 12-month period, measured from the lowest gross rental rate charged during the prior 12 months. For the same tenant, rent may not be increased in more than two increments in a 12-month period; initial rent for a new tenancy is not capped, and local stricter rent control continues to govern where applicable.
rules.key_value: lesser of 5% + cost of living change or 10% in any 12-month period; no more than 2 increases in 12 months
rules.coverage_conditions: Covered residential real property subject to the statewide cap.; The cap applies only after the owner establishes the initial rent for a new tenancy in which no prior tenant remains in lawful possession.
rules.exemptions: Affordable or subsidized housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction, recorded document, or subsidy agreement is exempt.; Dormitories owned and operated by schools are exempt.; Housing already subject to stricter public rent or price control is exempt from the state cap.; Housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years is exempt, unless it is a mobilehome.; Separately alienable residential real property, including a mobilehome, is exempt if ownership and notice conditions are met.; The owner must not be a real estate investment trust.; The owner must not be a corporation.; The owner must not be an LLC with at least one corporate member.; The owner must not be management of a mobilehome park.; Required exemption notice must be provided to tenants.; A duplex-like property with two separate dwelling units in one structure is exempt if the owner occupied one unit as principal residence at the beginning of the tenancy, continues in occupancy, and neither unit is an ADU or JADU.; Owner occupied one unit as principal residence at the beginning of the tenancy and continues in occupancy.
rules.interaction:
(d) (3) Housing subject to rent or price control through a public entity’s valid exercise of its police power consistent with Chapter 2.7 (commencing with Section 1954.50) that restricts annual increases in the rental rate to an amount less than that provided in subdivision (a).

(m) (2) It is the intent of the Legislature that this section should apply only for the limited time needed to address the current statewide housing crisis, as described in paragraph (1). This section is not intended to expand or limit the authority of local governments to establish local policies regulating rents consistent with Chapter 2.7 (commencing with Section 1954.50), nor is it a statement regarding the appropriate, allowable rental rate increase when a local government adopts a policy regulating rent that is otherwise consistent with Chapter 2.7 (commencing with Section 1954.50).
(3) Nothing in this section authorizes a local government to establish limitations on any rental rate increases not otherwise permissible under Chapter 2.7 (commencing with Section 1954.50), or affects the existing authority of a local government to adopt or maintain rent controls or price controls consistent with that chapter.
rules.quoted_span: (a) (1)   Subject to subdivision (b), an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, of the lowest gross rental rate charged for that dwelling or unit at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2024-01-01 (effective date of the 2023 amendment adding current text, D024); 2019-03-15 (applies to covered rent increases occurring on or after this date, except mobilehome timing in subdivision (i), D024); 2021-02-18 (mobilehome-specific applicability date, D024)
rules.penalty: An owner who demands, accepts, receives, or retains rent above the maximum allowed is liable for injunctive relief, damages equal to the overcharge, attorney’s fees and costs, and potentially up to treble damages for willful or oppressive conduct.

rules.title: Statewide just-cause eviction requirements
rules.requirement: After qualifying occupancy periods, an owner may not terminate a residential tenancy without stated just cause. The statute defines at-fault and no-fault causes, requires cure notices for curable lease violations, mandates relocation assistance or final-month rent waiver for no-fault terminations, and specifies exemptions and local-ordinance interaction.
rules.key_value: Just cause required after 12 months' lawful occupancy; relocation assistance or rent waiver = 1 month's rent for no-fault terminations
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied the property for 12 months, or in certain multi-adult tenancies all tenants have occupied for 12 months or one or more tenants for 24 months.
rules.exemptions: Transient and tourist hotel occupancy.; Housing accommodations in specified nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care, elderly care, or adult residential facilities.; Dormitories owned and operated by specified schools.; Tenant shares bathroom or kitchen facilities with owner who maintains principal residence at the property.; Single-family owner-occupied residences where owner-occupant rents or leases no more than two units or bedrooms, including an ADU or JADU.; Owner-occupant rents or leases no more than two units or bedrooms in the single-family owner-occupied residence.; A mobilehome under the single-family owner-occupied residences exemption.; Property contains two separate dwelling units within a single structure.; Owner occupied one unit as principal residence at beginning of tenancy and continues in occupancy.; Neither unit is an accessory dwelling unit or junior accessory dwelling unit.; Housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, unless the housing is a mobilehome.; Residential real property alienable separate from title to any other dwelling unit, including a mobilehome, if owner-type and notice conditions are met.; Owner is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with at least one corporate member, or management of a mobilehome park.; Tenant received the statutory written exemption notice, with timing rules for existing, commenced, or renewed tenancies.; Housing restricted or subsidized as affordable housing for very low, low, or moderate income households.; Residential real property subject to a qualifying local just-cause ordinance.; Homeowner of a mobilehome.
rules.interaction:
(i) (1) This section does not apply to the following residential real property:
(A) Residential real property subject to a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy adopted on or before September 1, 2019, in which case the local ordinance shall apply.
(B) Residential real property subject to a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy adopted or amended after September 1, 2019, that is more protective than this section, in which case the local ordinance shall apply.
(2) A residential real property shall not be subject to both a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy and this section.
(3) A local ordinance adopted
after September 1, 2019, that is less protective than this section shall not be enforced unless this section is repealed.
rules.quoted_span: (a) Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2026-01-01 (amendment effective date, D023)
rules.penalty: An owner who attempts to recover possession in material violation is liable for actual damages, discretionary attorney’s fees and costs, and up to three times actual damages or punitive damages for willful or oppressive conduct; the Attorney General and local city attorney or county counsel may seek injunctive relief.

rules.title: California security deposit cap for residential tenancies
rules.requirement: For residential property used as the tenant’s dwelling, a landlord generally may not demand or receive security exceeding one month’s rent, plus first month’s rent paid on or before initial occupancy. A small-landlord exception allows up to two months’ rent if the landlord is a natural person or qualifying LLC and owns no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four total dwelling units; this exception does not apply to service members.
rules.key_value: General cap: 1 month’s rent; small-landlord exception: 2 months’ rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property used as the tenant's dwelling.
rules.exemptions: Advance payment of at least six months' rent for a lease term of six months or longer is not prohibited by the cap.; Mutual agreements for specified-fee alterations requested by the tenant are not precluded by the cap.; Small-landlord exception requires the landlord to be a natural person or an LLC whose members are all natural persons.; Small-landlord exception requires ownership of no more than two residential rental properties.; Small-landlord exception requires the properties collectively to include no more than four dwelling units offered for rent.; Small-landlord two-month exception does not apply if the prospective tenant is a service member.; The deposit-cap subdivision does not apply to security collected or demanded before July 1, 2024.
rules.quoted_span: Except as provided in paragraph (2), (3), or (5), a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2025-04-01 (Special rule for written statement and return of additional security for service members when higher than standard or advertised security is charged., D025); 2024-07-01 (Deposit-cap subdivision does not apply to security collected or demanded before this date., D025)
rules.penalty: Bad faith claim or retention of the security may subject the landlord to statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages.

rules.title: California application screening fee limits and procedures
rules.requirement: California allows landlords or their agents to charge an application screening fee only to cover actual screening costs, subject to a statutory cap and specific process, receipt, refund, and credit-report rules. The fee cannot be charged when no unit is or will soon be available, and the landlord must use one of two compliant screening/refund processes.
rules.key_value: Actual out-of-pocket costs; not more than $30 per applicant, annually CPI-adjusted beginning January 1, 1998
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies when a landlord or agent receives a request to rent a residential property from an applicant.
rules.exemptions: No screening fee may be charged when the landlord knows or should know no unit is available then or within a reasonable time.; The section is not intended to preempt deposit and fee rules under federal or state housing assistance programs.
rules.interaction:
(k) The application screening fee shall not be considered an “advance fee” as that term is used in Section 10026 of the Business and Professions Code, and shall not be considered “security” as that term is used in Section 1950.5.

(l) This section is not intended
to preempt any provisions or regulations that govern the collection of deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs.
rules.quoted_span:
(b) The amount of the application screening fee shall not be greater than the actual
out-of-pocket costs of gathering information concerning the applicant, including, but not limited to, the cost of using a tenant screening service or a consumer credit reporting service, and the reasonable value of time spent by the landlord or their agent in obtaining information on the applicant. In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant. The thirty dollar ($30) application screening fee may be adjusted annually by the landlord or their agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning on January 1, 1998.

rules.title: Fair housing screening restrictions based on source of income and subsidized-rent applicants
rules.requirement: California fair housing law prohibits housing discrimination based on source of income and bars certain screening practices for applicants with government rent subsidies. Landlords may not refuse subsidy-program compliance, may not use income standards that ignore the tenant-paid portion of subsidized rent, and if they use credit history for a subsidized applicant they must offer and reasonably consider lawful alternative evidence of ability to pay the tenant portion.
rules.key_value: Must base subsidized-rent income screening on tenant-paid portion; must offer alternative evidence if using credit history for subsidized applicants
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to owners of housing accommodations and persons or entities involved in rental housing decisions; Operative subsidized-applicant screening rules apply when there is a government rent subsidy
rules.exemptions: Owner may still request employment verification, landlord references, and identity verification; Inquiry about level or source of income is not itself source-of-income discrimination
rules.quoted_span:
(o) (1) In instances in which there is a government rent subsidy, to do either of the following:
(A) Use a financial or income standard in assessing eligibility for the rental of housing that is not based on the portion of the rent to be paid by the tenant.
(B) (i) Use a person’s credit history as part of the application process for a rental accommodation without offering the applicant the option, at the applicant’s discretion, of providing lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of the applicant’s reasonable ability to pay
the portion of the rent to be paid by the tenant, including, but not limited to, government benefit payments, pay records, and bank statements.
(ii) If the applicant elects to provide lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of the applicant’s
reasonable ability to pay pursuant to clause (i), the housing provider shall do both of the following:
(I) Provide the applicant reasonable time to respond with that alternative evidence.
(II) Reasonably consider that alternative evidence in lieu of the person’s credit history in determining whether to offer the rental accommodation to the applicant.

rules.title: Application screening fee timing and availability restrictions
rules.requirement: California limits when landlords may charge rental application screening fees. A landlord may not charge when no unit is available or reasonably expected to become available, and may charge only under one of two compliant screening processes: ordered consideration with fee charged only when the application is actually considered, or full refund to unselected applicants within stated deadlines.
rules.key_value: Fee only if unit available and either actual-consideration process or full-refund process; cap is actual out-of-pocket costs and no more than $30 plus CPI adjustment
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies when a landlord or agent receives a request to rent residential property from an applicant
rules.exemptions: Section does not preempt deposit and fee rules under federal or state housing assistance programs
rules.interaction:
(k) The application screening fee shall not be considered an “advance fee” as that term is used in Section 10026 of the Business and Professions Code, and shall not be considered “security” as that term is used in Section 1950.5.
(l) This section is not intended
to preempt any provisions or regulations that govern the collection of deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs.
rules.quoted_span: A landlord or their agent shall not charge an applicant an application screening fee when they know or should have known that no rental unit is available at that time or will be available within a reasonable period of time.

rules.title: Common pricing algorithms prohibited as part of antitrust conspiracy or coercive pricing
rules.requirement: California makes it unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, trust, or conspiracy restraining trade, and also prohibits using or distributing such an algorithm to coerce another person to adopt its recommended price or commercial term for the same or similar products or services in California. The statute defines common pricing algorithm broadly and states that antitrust laws still apply.
rules.key_value: Use/distribution of a "common pricing algorithm" is unlawful when used in antitrust conspiracy or coercive pricing; "common pricing algorithm" includes technology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term.
rules.interaction: (c) Nothing in this section shall impair or limit the applicability of antitrust laws.
rules.quoted_span:
16729.
(a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
(b) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm if the person coerces another person to set or adopt a recommended price or commercial term recommended by the common pricing algorithm for the same or similar products or services in the jurisdiction of this state.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2025-10-06 (approval and filing date, D022)
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents

rules.title: Algorithmic rent fixing in rental housing market prohibited
rules.requirement: Hoboken prohibits landlords renting residential dwelling units in the city from price fixing using algorithmic pricing, defined as using software, algorithms, or data-sharing platforms to collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information to coordinate, recommend, or implement rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels. Alleged violations may be brought by the Division of Housing or an aggrieved private citizen in Hoboken Municipal Court, and penalties may include those under N.J.S.A. 40:49-5, a fine up to $2,000, or community service up to 90 days.
rules.key_value: Fine up to $2,000; community service up to 90 days
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords who rent residential dwelling units used as a primary residence in Hoboken.
rules.exemptions: Does not cover medical/long-term care or detention facilities.
rules.quoted_span: Landlords who rent any residential dwelling unit (defined as any primary residence excluding medical/long-term care or detention facilities) in the City of Hoboken are prohibited from price fixing using algorithmic pricing. For purposes of this chapter, "price fixing using algorithmic pricing" shall be defined as the use of software, algorithms, or data-sharing platforms to collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information from other real estate lessors in order to coordinate, recommend, or implement rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units among competing real estate lessors.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2025-07 (secondary source states effective month, S002)
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents
rules.penalty: Penalties as prescribed under N.J.S.A. 40:49-5; a fine not exceeding $2,000; or a period of community service not exceeding 90 days.

rules.title: Residential security deposit and upfront payment limits
rules.requirement: For residential tenancies, a landlord or the landlord's agent may not require more than first month's rent, last month's rent at the same rate, a security deposit equal to the first month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock. The statute also authorizes regulations allowing an optional fee in lieu of a security deposit, with the total fee capped at no more than 1 month's rent.

rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential tenancies and leases relating to residential real property.; Applies at or prior to the commencement of any tenancy.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to any lease, rental, occupancy or tenancy of 100 days or less for a vacation or recreational purpose.
rules.interaction: provided, however, that the executive office of housing and livable communities may promulgate regulations to authorize a lessor and a tenant or prospective tenant to agree to the payment of a fee in lieu of payment of a security deposit

(i) rent for the first full month of occupancy;  and,
(ii) rent for the last full month of occupancy calculated at the same rate as the first month;  and,
(iii) a security deposit equal to the first month's rent provided that such security deposit is deposited as required by subsection (3) and that the tenant is given the statement of condition as required by subsection (2);  provided, however, that the executive office of housing and livable communities may promulgate regulations to authorize a lessor and a tenant or prospective tenant to agree to the payment of a fee in lieu of payment of a security deposit;

rules.requirement: New Jersey generally allows eviction from covered residential rental property only for statutory good cause, with specified notice requirements that vary by cause. consent of the tenants or through the legal process of eviction.

rules.title: Prohibition of Anti-Competitive Automated Rent Price-Fixing Ordinance
rules.requirement: San Diego proposed an ordinance to prohibit selling, licensing, or otherwise providing an algorithmic device to a landlord, and to prohibit landlords from using an algorithmic device to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property. The proposal defines covered software as a product using algorithms and nonpublic competitor data to advise or recommend rental rates or occupancy levels, with specified exclusions for certain reporting tools and affordable-housing compliance tools.
rules.key_value: Up to $1,000 per violation; each month and each residential rental property can be a separate violation
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental property in the City of San Diego.
rules.exemptions: Excludes software or products publishing aggregated historical nonpublic competitor data more than 90 days old or public information, if they do not recommend future rental rates or occupancy levels.; Excludes software or products used to establish rental rates or income limits under affordable housing program guidelines.
rules.interaction:
(b) The remedies under section 98.1104 are cumulative and are in addition to

rules.citation: San Diego Municipal Code §§ 98.1101–98.1104 (proposed by Ordinance O-2025-107)
rules.quoted_span:
§98.1103  Use and Sale of Algorithmic Devices Prohibited
(a) It is unlawful for a person to sell, license, or otherwise provide an
algorithmic device to a landlord.
(b) It is unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device to set rental rates
or occupancy levels for residential rental property.
For each month a violation of section 98.1103(b) exists or continues, and
for each residential rental property a landlord uses an algorithmic device,
it shall constitute a separate and distinct violation.

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance annual allowable rent increase for rent-controlled units
rules.requirement: For rent-controlled units, San Francisco sets an annual allowable rent increase amount. For the period March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027, the allowable increase is 1.6%. Some tenancies exempt from the Rent Ordinance's rent increase limitations remain subject to the Ordinance's eviction protections. The document identifies newly constructed rental units with first certificates of occupancy after June 13, 1979, Costa-Hawkins-eligible tenancies, and some tenancies regulated by another government agency as examples.
rules.key_value: 1.6% for March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rent-controlled units.
rules.quoted_span: For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable increase amount effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 1.6%.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2027-02-28 (end of stated effective period, D080); 2025-03-01 (prior annual allowable increase period begins, D080); 2026-02-28 (prior annual allowable increase period ends, D080)

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance just-cause eviction requirements
rules.requirement: For rental units covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord may evict only for one of 17 just-cause reasons, and expiration of a rental agreement or change in ownership is not just cause. The same just-cause requirement also applies to removal of certain housing services. For tenants evicted under the Ellis Act, relocation payments are due in the amounts set by the Rent Board schedule based on the date the eviction notice is served. For notices served from March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027, the payment is $11,110.05 per tenant, capped at $33,330.13 per unit, plus $7,443.90 for each elderly or disabled tenant.
rules.key_value: 17 just-cause reasons
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental units covered by the Rent Ordinance; Some tenancies exempt from rent increase limits are still covered by the eviction provisions; Newly constructed rental units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979 are still subject to the eviction provisions; Tenancies eligible for a rent increase under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act are still subject to the eviction provisions; Some tenancies where rent is regulated by another government agency are still subject to the eviction provisions
rules.interaction: Some tenancies that are exempt from the rent increase limitations of the Ordinance are still subject to the eviction provisions of the Ordinance, and tenants in these categories can only be evicted for one of the “just cause” reasons listed in the Ordinance. This includes tenancies in newly constructed rental units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, tenancies that are eligible for a rent increase under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act, and some tenancies where the rent is regulated by another government agency.
rules.quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction. Note that the mere expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership does not constitute "just cause" for eviction.
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents
rules.penalty: If a landlord evicts or tries to evict a tenant unlawfully, the landlord may be subject to substantial civil and/or criminal liability.

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance relocation payments for specified no-fault evictions
rules.requirement: For evictions based on owner/relative move-in, demolition/permanent removal from housing use, temporary capital improvement work, or substantial rehabilitation, relocation payments are due in the amounts set by the Rent Board schedule based on the date the eviction notice is served. For notices served from March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027, the payment is $8,245.00 per tenant, capped at $24,733.00 per unit, plus $5,497.00 for each elderly or disabled tenant or household with minor children.
rules.key_value: 3/01/26–2/28/27: $8,245 per tenant; $24,733 max per unit; +$5,497 protected-household add-on
rules.coverage_conditions: Evictions based on owner/relative move-in, demolition/permanent removal of unit from housing use, temporary capital improvement work, or substantial rehabilitation
rules.exemptions: Temporary capital improvement evictions for less than 20 days are governed by California Civil Code Section 1947.9 instead of Rent Ordinance Section 37.9C
rules.interaction: *The amount of relocation payments for temporary capital improvement evictions for less than 20 days is governed by California Civil Code Section 1947.9 and not by Rent Ordinance Section 37.9C.

rules.title: Algorithmic rent-setting ban
rules.requirement: San Francisco added a Rent Ordinance provision prohibiting the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco. The law defines an algorithmic device as software using algorithms to analyze nonpublic competitor rental data to recommend rents for vacant units, and it allows tenant or City Attorney civil actions for violations.
rules.key_value: Prohibits sale or use of algorithmic devices for residential rent-setting or occupancy management
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential units in San Francisco.
rules.quoted_span: The law prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2024-10 (secondary source summary of effective month, S002)
rules.penalty: Allows a tenant or the City Attorney to bring a civil action for violations.

rules.title: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization Ordinance rent increase cap
rules.requirement: Santa Ana limits annual residential rent increases to the lesser of 3% or 80% of the percent change in CPI over the most recent 12-month period; if CPI is negative, no rent increase is permitted. The City publishes the annual allowable increase, effective September 1 each year after the initial publication.
rules.key_value: lesser of 3% per year or 80% of CPI change; if CPI is negative, 0%
rules.exemptions: Residential buildings constructed after February 1, 1995 are exempt from the rent cap.; Mobile home spaces offered for rent after January 1, 1990 are exempt from the rent cap.
rules.quoted_span: Increase in residential rents are limited to the lower of 3% per year, or 80% of the percent change in the Consumer Price Index over the most recent 12-month period. If the CPI is negative, no rent increase is permitted.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2021-09-01 (annual published allowable rent increase effective date in subsequent years, D085)

rules.title: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
rules.requirement: After 30 days, an owner may not terminate a tenancy without just cause stated in a written notice. The ordinance includes at-fault and no-fault causes, requires notice and an opportunity to cure before a just-cause termination notice, and requires relocation assistance or rent waiver for no-fault terminations.
rules.key_value: Just cause required after 30 days; 3 months relocation assistance or final 3 months' rent waived for no-fault terminations
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies after the first 30 days of tenancy.
rules.exemptions: Housing produced in the last 15 years is excluded.; Deed-restricted affordable housing is excluded.; Hotel and transient occupancy are excluded.; Hospital and care facilities are excluded.; Dormitories are excluded.; Other shared living quarters are excluded.
rules.citation: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: After 30 days, an owner shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in a written notice.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2021-12-19 (deadline for notice to existing tenants, D085)
rules.raw_citation: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
